title-group.article-title: Effect of Rifampicin on the Pharmacokinetics of Valemetostat and Its Primary Metabolite: A Phase 1 Study in Healthy Participants

abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat) is a dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH)2 and EZH1, approved in Japan for the treatment of relapsed or refractory peripheral T‐cell lymphoma, including adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma, and globally under investigation for the treatment of non‐Hodgkin lymphomas and solid tumors. Valemetostat is a substrate of cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A) and P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp) in vitro. This phase 1, open‐label, single‐sequence crossover study assessed the effect of repeated oral doses of rifampicin, a strong CYP3A and P‐gp inducer, on the pharmacokinetics (PK) of valemetostat in healthy Japanese participants. In this trial, 20 participants received two doses of valemetostat 200 mg, once alone and once after repeated daily doses of rifampicin 600 mg. Coadministration with rifampicin decreased the maximum plasma concentration (C max) and area under the plasma concentration–time curve extrapolated to infinity (AUCinf) of total valemetostat. The geometric least‐squares mean ratios (GMR, test/reference) for C max and AUCinf were 0.417 [90% confidence interval (CI), 0.319–0.545] and 0.286 [90% CI, 0.225–0.364], respectively. C max of CALZ‐1809a (a major valemetostat oxidative metabolite) increased (GMR, 1.287 [90% CI, 1.036–1.600]), while the AUCinf decreased (GMR, 0.713 [90% CI, 0.573–0.886]). No treatment‐related or Grade ≥ 2 adverse events were reported. These results showed that valemetostat exposure was reduced upon coadministration of rifampicin, suggesting that concomitant use of valemetostat with strong CYP3A and P‐gp inducers should be avoided.

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Valemetostat is an oral, potent, dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH)2 and EZH1, which has recently been approved in Japan for the treatment of relapsed/refractory peripheral T‐cell lymphoma, including adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma. Valemetostat is a substrate of cytochrome P450 3A (CYP3A) and P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp). Valemetostat's maximum plasma concentration (C max) and plasma concentration–time curve (AUC) are increased by CYP3A and P‐gp inhibitors like itraconazole.

What question did this study address? ○
This phase 1 drug–drug interaction trial assessed the pharmacokinetics of valemetostat when coadministered with rifampicin, a strong CYP3A and P‐gp inducer, to inform dosing recommendations when valemetostat is used concomitantly with CYP3A or P‐gp inducers.

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
Coadministration of valemetostat with rifampicin decreased C max and AUC from time 0 to infinity of total valemetostat by approximately 60% and 70%, respectively.

How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science? ○
The outcomes of this study indicate that concomitant use of valemetostat and strong CYP3A and P‐gp inducers, including rifampicin, should be avoided.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Valemetostat tosylate (valemetostat) is an oral, potent, and selective dual inhibitor of enhancer of zeste homolog (EZH)2 and EZH1. Overexpression or gain‐of‐function mutations of EZH2 have been reported to be associated with tumorigenesis and progression of non‐Hodgkin lymphomas (NHLs) [1, 2, 3]. Dual inhibition of EZH2 and EZH1 by valemetostat maximally suppresses the aberrant trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 27 (H3K27me3), increasing the expression of silenced genes, including those associated with the regulation of cell proliferation and differentiation [1, 2, 4, 5].

Valemetostat is approved in Japan for the treatment of relapsed or refractory (R/R) adult T‐cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL), and R/R peripheral T‐cell lymphoma (PTCL) [6, 7]. In the phase 2 DS3201‐A‐J201 and DS3201‐A‐U202 clinical trials, daily treatment with 200 mg valemetostat demonstrated considerable efficacy and a favorable tolerability and safety profile [8, 9]. Valemetostat is currently in clinical development for the treatment of other types of lymphoma and solid tumors.

In vitro studies have demonstrated that valemetostat is a substrate of cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A, which is predominantly expressed in the liver and small intestine, and of P‐glycoprotein (P‐gp), which is mainly expressed on the apical side of gastrointestinal epithelial cells (data on file). In a phase 1 drug–drug interaction (DDI) study of valemetostat in healthy Japanese participants, concomitant administration with itraconazole (a P‐gp inhibitor and strong CYP3A inhibitor) increased the maximum plasma concentration (C max) and exposure (area under the plasma concentration–time curve extrapolated to infinity [AUCinf]) of valemetostat by 2.9‐fold and 4.2‐fold, respectively. When valemetostat was administered with fluconazole (a moderate CYP3A inhibitor), both the C max and AUCinf of valemetostat increased by ~1.6‐fold each [10]. These findings demonstrate that in the presence of CYP3A or P‐gp modulators, the pharmacokinetics (PK) of valemetostat are likely to be altered due to DDIs.

The primary objective of the present study was to evaluate the effects of repeated oral doses of rifampicin on the PK of valemetostat in healthy Japanese participants. Rifampicin, an antibiotic used to treat antibacterial infections including tuberculosis associated with cancer or its treatments, is commonly employed in DDI studies of oral anticancer drugs, since it is a strong inducer of CYP3A and P‐gp [11, 12, 13]. The safety of concomitant use of valemetostat and rifampicin was evaluated as a secondary objective, and the outcomes were used to inform dose adjustment recommendations.

sec.title: Study Design
sec.p: This study was a phase 1, open‐label, single‐sequence crossover clinical trial, conducted at Souseikai Fukuoka Mirai Hospital in Fukuoka, Japan. The clinical trial followed the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Council for Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use Consolidated Guideline E6 for Good Clinical Practice, and local regulatory requirements. The study protocol was approved by the local institutional review board (IRB) (Hakata Clinic IRB; Approval No. 1776P1CP‐3, dated on 2020‐06‐19), and the trial was registered to the Japan Registry of Clinical Trials. Written informed consent was obtained from participants prior to screening.

sec.title: Study Participants
sec.p: The study enrolled healthy Japanese males and females of 20–45 years of age and a body mass index (BMI) of ≥ 18.5 and < 25.0 kg/m2 at screening. Medical history, physical examinations, vital signs, 12‐lead electrocardiograms (ECGs), and clinical laboratory tests were assessed to further evaluate study eligibility. Participants with clinically significant diseases, including cardiovascular, respiratory, blood, hematopoietic, gastrointestinal, or central nervous system disorders, hepatic/renal impairment, thyroid dysfunction, pituitary malfunction, adrenal insufficiency, allergy or hypersensitivity history, alcohol‐ or drug‐dependence, or a positive test for infections such as human immunodeficiency virus or hepatitis, were excluded from the study. Use or planned use of medications (including supplements containing St. John's Wort, which is known for inducing CYP3A) other than the study drug from 30 days before hospital admission until the post‐study or follow‐up examination was also prohibited. Complete inclusion and exclusion criteria are reported in the Supporting Information.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: Participants received a single oral dose of 200 mg valemetostat on Day 1 after 10 h of fasting. The 200 mg/day dose is clinically recommended for R/R ATLL and PTCL. A PK‐pharmacodynamic analysis demonstrated that the inhibition of H3K27me3 in surrogate tissues, such as granulocytes, was near maximum at the mean AUC at steady state during valemetostat 200 mg/day treatment [14]. Rifampicin was administered orally at a dose of 600 mg once daily for 15 days from Day 8 to Day 22. Participants received another single oral dose of 200 mg valemetostat on Day 16 after fasting for at least 10 h and 2 h after administration of rifampicin (Figure 1). A single oral dose of 200 mg valemetostat was selected based on findings from prior clinical studies in healthy Japanese adults and patients with R/R NHL, confirming it to be safe and tolerable [10, 15]. A rifampicin dose of 600 mg once daily was selected based on its approved dosage in Japan and use in previous DDI studies [16, 17, 18]. Fasting conditions were used for the administration of both valemetostat and rifampicin due to the reported impact of fed conditions on drug absorption [10, 16, 19]. Administration of a second oral dose of 200 mg valemetostat on Day 16 (the ninth day of rifampicin administration) was selected based on findings demonstrating the maximum level of CYP3A induction by rifampicin after approximately 7 days of consecutive administration [20]. Study participants remained in the hospital from the day before the first dose of valemetostat until the final dose of rifampicin, accounting for a period of 23 nights and 24 days. Participants were prohibited from intake of caffeine‐based beverages, grapefruit, alcohol, smoking, or engaging in excessive physical exercise during their hospital stay and until follow‐up examinations on Days 35–37. All study drugs were taken with 240 mL of water, and participants were instructed to remain in a sitting position for 4 h after administration of valemetostat.

sec.title: PK Analyses
sec.p: The primary PK endpoints were C max, AUC up to the last quantifiable timepoint (AUClast), and AUCinf of total (bound + unbound) valemetostat when administered alone and when coadministered with rifampicin. Secondary endpoints for PK analysis during administration of valemetostat alone and coadministration with rifampicin included time to reach C max (T max), elimination rate constant associated with the terminal phase (K el), terminal elimination half‐life (t 1/2), oral clearance (CL/F), and apparent volume of distribution (Vz/F) of total valemetostat concentration and C max, AUClast, AUCinf, T max, K el, and t 1/2 of CALZ‐1809a, an oxidative metabolite of valemetostat. C max, AUClast, AUCinf, T max, K el, and t 1/2 of unbound valemetostat during administration of valemetostat alone were also secondary endpoints.

Blood samples were collected on Day 1 and Day 9, before administration, and at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, 24, 48, 72, 96, and 168 h post‐dose. Concentrations of total and unbound valemetostat, as well as CALZ‐1809a, were analyzed in plasma samples using validated liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry methods. For measurement of total and unbound valemetostat, refer to Tachibana et al. [10]. For CALZ‐1809a, a 10‐μL aliquot of plasma sample was mixed with an equal volume of acetonitrile. Then, 10 μL of 0.1% (v/v) trifluoroacetic acid in water was added. Next, it was mixed with 100 μL of acetonitrile containing deuterium‐labeled CALZ‐1809a (CALZ‐1809‐d6) as an internal standard for protein precipitation. After centrifugation, the supernatant was mixed with 250 μL of water and injected on an ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (2.1 mm I.D. × 50 mm, particle size 1.7 μm, Waters Corp.) for mass spectrometric detection (API5500 triple quadrupole mass spectrometer [Sciex]). Mass spectrometric detection was done using positive mode and Turbo‐IonSpray as the source. The lower limit of quantification and the validated concentration range for CALZ‐1809a were 1 ng/mL and 1–1000 ng/mL, respectively. The within‐ and inter‐day assay precision (percent coefficient of variation) for quality control samples were in the ranges of 1.0%–11.8% and 2.0%–12.1%, respectively, and the assay accuracy percentages were in the ranges of 95.2%–118.0% and 101.0%–107.0%, respectively.
PK parameters for valemetostat and CALZ‐1809a were calculated via a noncompartmental analysis using Phoenix WinNonlin version 8.1 (Certara).

sec.title: Safety Assessments
sec.p: Safety assessments included monitoring of treatment‐emergent adverse events (TEAEs), clinical laboratory parameters, body weights, vital signs (blood pressure, pulse rate, and body temperature), and ECGs. The severity of TEAEs was assessed according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events Version 5.0 Japanese edition by the Japan Clinical Oncology Group. TEAEs were evaluated from the first dose of valemetostat until the end of the follow‐up period (Days 35–37). Collection of blood and urine samples for the safety assessments was done on Day 1 pre‐dose; Day 2, 5, 8, 9, and 12; Day 16 pre‐dose; Day 17, 20, and 23; and at follow‐up or withdrawal (Days 35–37). Vital signs and ECGs were assessed on Day 1, 2, 8, 16, 17, and 23 and at follow‐up or withdrawal.

sec.title: Statistical Analyses
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using Version 9.4 of the Statistical Analysis System (SAS). PK parameters (C max, AUClast, and AUCinf) of total valemetostat and CALZ‐1809a were analyzed using a linear mixed‐effect model analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the natural logarithms as response variables, treatment periods as fixed effects, and participants as random effects. The natural logarithms were inversely transformed, and the geometric least‐squares (LS) mean ratio of the Test (Period B; valemetostat with rifampicin) to Reference (Period A; valemetostat alone) and its two‐sided 90% confidence interval (CI) were calculated.

sec.title: Demographic and Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: A total of 20 healthy participants (14 males and 6 females) were enrolled and completed the study (Table 1). Participants had a mean (range) age of 30.5 (20–45) years, with a mean (standard deviation [SD]) weight of 57.30 (7.090) kg and mean (SD) BMI of 20.77 (1.169) kg/m2. One participant had a medical history of appendicitis and appendicectomy.

sec.title: PK Analyses
sec.p: Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the mean plasma concentration–time profiles of valemetostat and its metabolite, CALZ‐1809a, when valemetostat is administered alone and coadministered with rifampicin. Median (range) T max of valemetostat was 3.00 (1.00–5.00) h when administered alone and 4.00 (1.50–6.00) h after coadministration with rifampicin (Table 2). For CALZ‐1809a, median (range) T max was 5.00 (2.00–6.00) h and 4.50 (3.00–8.00) h after administration of valemetostat alone and valemetostat with rifampicin, respectively. The mean (SD) t 1/2 of total valemetostat was 22.6 (2.98) h after administration of valemetostat alone and 18.3 (5.93) h after concomitant administration of rifampicin. Mean (SD) t 1/2 of CALZ‐1809a was 36.9 (5.41) h after administration of valemetostat alone and 38.3 (11.4) h after coadministration of valemetostat with rifampicin. Mean (SD) C max of total valemetostat was reduced after coadministration with rifampicin (627 (351) ng/mL), compared with valemetostat alone (1490 (730) ng/mL). In contrast, mean (SD) C max of CALZ‐1809a increased upon concomitant administration of valemetostat and rifampicin (622 (295) ng/mL), compared with valemetostat alone (472 (184) ng/mL). The mean AUClast and AUCinf of total valemetostat and CALZ‐1809a were decreased with the coadministration of valemetostat and rifampicin, compared with valemetostat alone. The mean metabolite‐to‐parent ratio (MR) based on the molecular weight adjusted AUCinf of CALZ‐1809a and valemetostat increased from 1.17 after administration of valemetostat alone, to 2.89 after coadministration of valemetostat and rifampicin. The geometric LS mean ratios of C max, AUClast, and AUCinf were 0.417, 0.288, and 0.286 for total valemetostat and 1.287, 0.716, and 0.713 for CALZ‐1809a, respectively, when valemetostat was administered concomitantly with rifampicin, compared with valemetostat alone (Table 3). For unbound valemetostat, the median T max was 3.50 h and the mean C max, AUClast, and AUCinf were 109 ng/mL, 551 ng·h/mL, and 560 ng·h/mL, respectively, after administration of valemetostat alone (Figure S1 and Table S1). The mean t 1/2 was 21.3 h for unbound valemetostat. The fraction unbound (fu) of valemetostat was in the mean range of 0.0484–0.0625 after administration of valemetostat alone.

sec.title: Safety Assessment
sec.p: All 20 participants received valemetostat alone and valemetostat with rifampicin and were included in the safety analyses. TEAEs were recorded in 5 participants (25.0%), of whom 1 (5.0%) had TEAEs after administration of rifampicin alone (from Days 8 to 16), 2 (10.0%) after concurrent administration of valemetostat and rifampicin (from Days 16 to 23), and 2 (10.0%) after discharge (Day 23) (Table S2). All reported TEAEs were of Grade 1, with no incidence of TEAEs of higher grades, serious TEAEs, TEAEs that required study withdrawal, or deaths. No TEAEs were recorded after administration of valemetostat alone. Only one TEAE (Grade 1 laryngeal pain) after coadministration of valemetostat and rifampicin was considered treatment‐related. No treatment‐related clinically significant changes were observed in the mean values of hematology, blood chemistry, urinalysis, vital signs, and ECGs (Table S3).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: DDIs may considerably influence the PK of drugs, altering their safety and efficacy. The main mechanisms behind PK DDIs involve the inhibition and/or induction of drug‐metabolizing enzymes and of transporters mediating the disposal of the victim drug [21, 22]. Valemetostat is a substrate of the CYP3A enzyme and P‐gp transporter and is therefore likely to be a victim drug during DDIs. This study reported, for the first time, the DDI of valemetostat and rifampicin, a strong CYP3A and P‐gp inducer, when administered concurrently.

Coadministration of valemetostat and rifampicin resulted in decreases in the C max and AUCs of total valemetostat by approximately 60% and 70%, respectively. This suggests that induction of CYP3A and/or P‐gp by rifampicin increases metabolic clearance of valemetostat and/or its intestinal excretion, thereby decreasing its systemic exposure. In contrast, the difference in the mean t 1/2 values of total valemetostat was relatively small between valemetostat administered alone and together with rifampicin. These outcomes suggest that rifampicin‐mediated CYP3A and/or P‐gp induction has considerable effect on the first‐pass elimination of valemetostat and consequently, on its availability in the gastrointestinal tract. Since the expression of CYP3A and P‐gp is regulated by the pregnane xenobiotic receptor (PXR) and the constitutive androstane receptor (CAR), most CYP3A inducers also up‐regulate the expression of drug transporters, including the ABCB1/MDR1 gene, which encodes P‐gp [23, 24]. Lutz et al. [25] compared the AUC ratios of various probe substrates of CYP3A and P‐gp when coadministered with the known CYP3A/P‐gp inducer rifampicin. The authors found that the induction of P‐gp by rifampicin is less pronounced than that of CYP3A, meaning that P‐gp inducers are one DDI category weaker than CYP3A [25]. This finding is in agreement with our investigation of the DDI liability for valemetostat, using physiologically‐based PK modeling, in which the effect of rifampicin on valemetostat C max and AUC was well‐reproduced by the model when induction of intestinal CYP3A and P‐gp were both considered [26]. Together, these data suggest that the decrease in valemetostat exposure by rifampicin is likely due to its induction of CYP3A, and to a lesser extent, the induction of P‐gp in the intestine.

In a previously published exposure–response analysis of valemetostat in patients with R/R ATLL, the target exposure range for unbound valemetostat was established by defining a modified region of practical equivalence (ROPE, 184–887 ng·h/mL), which was expected to provide satisfactory efficacy and acceptable safety at the clinically recommended dose of 200 mg/day [27]. This DDI study found that coadministration with rifampicin decreased the AUC of total valemetostat by 70%, suggesting a similar decrease in AUC of unbound valemetostat, which results in valemetostat exposure falling below the target exposure defined by the ROPE. Therefore, to ensure optimal efficacy and safety outcomes, concurrent use of valemetostat and a strong CYP3A and P‐gp inducer should be avoided.

The DDI study also assessed the impact of rifampicin on the valemetostat metabolite, CALZ‐1809a. CALZ‐1809a is an oxidized form of valemetostat at the dimethylpyridinone ring. A recently reported open‐label, phase 1, clinical study (DS3201‐A‐U105) demonstrated that CALZ‐1809a is the primary metabolite of valemetostat, and in vitro metabolism studies have shown that the formation and metabolism of CALZ‐1809a involve the enzyme CYP3A4/5 (data on file). Hence, rifampicin‐mediated induction of CYP3A directly impacted the production and elimination of CALZ‐1809a. As a result, after administration of valemetostat with repeated doses of rifampicin, the C max of CALZ‐1809a was increased by approximately 30% due to increased first‐pass metabolism, and AUCs decreased by approximately 30%, compared to valemetostat when administered alone. In addition, coadministration with rifampicin increased the mean MR of CALZ‐1809a to valemetostat, but the mean t 1/2 remained unchanged. These results suggest that the first‐pass metabolism of valemetostat by CYP3A increased and that the intestinal absorption of valemetostat decreased due to CYP3A and P‐gp induction by rifampicin.

This study also reports the PK of unbound valemetostat in healthy Japanese individuals during administration of valemetostat alone. For unbound valemetostat, median T max was 3.50 h and the mean t 1/2 was 21.3 h, both of which were close to the respective values for total valemetostat (Table S1). The C max and AUCs for unbound valemetostat were comparable to those previously reported in patients with ATLL after a single dose administration of 200 mg valemetostat on Cycle 1 Day 1 [8]. In contrast, the exposure of total valemetostat was lower in healthy participants. This could be partly explained by the concentration‐dependent plasma protein binding of valemetostat, which has a high affinity for alpha‐1‐acid glycoprotein (AAG) [28]. AAG is an acute phase protein, and the levels of AAG increase during inflammatory and/or disease states, such as malignant tumors [29, 30, 31]. In fact, the mean (SD) level of AAG at baseline was 50.7 (8.32) mg/dL in healthy participants (this study), and 94.0 (50.1) mg/dL in patients with ATLL (J201 study, data on file). The fu of valemetostat observed at various timepoints was slightly higher in healthy participants (mean range: 0.048–0.063) than with that observed in patients with ATLL (mean range: 0.029–0.052, data on file). In the population PK analysis, AAG was the most influential covariate for total valemetostat exposure; the difference in total valemetostat exposure between heathy individuals and patients with NHL was explained by fu and AAG levels [27]. However, protein binding had little impact on unbound valemetostat exposure.
With respect to safety, no Grade ≥ 2 TEAEs were reported in this study, indicating no safety concerns upon coadministration of valemetostat and rifampicin.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study demonstrated a substantial decrease in valemetostat exposure after coadministration of valemetostat with rifampicin, a strong CYP3A and P‐gp inducer. Although no safety signals were observed, based on the DDI response outcomes, concomitant use of valemetostat with strong CYP3A and P‐gp inducers, such as rifampicin, should be avoided.
